mc.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches pancreatic cells to hormones?
options: Alpha cells — ADH; beta cells — cortisol
Both cell types — thyroxine only
Beta cells — glucagon; alpha cells — insulin
Beta cells — insulin; alpha cells — glucagon
mc.answer: Beta cells — insulin; alpha cells — glucagon
mc.explanation: Cell identity and hormone role must stay linked.

mc.prompt: Between meals, glucagon helps maintain blood glucose mainly by…
options: Blocking every form of liver glucose release
Turning the thyroid into a pancreas
Promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production
Moving glucose into the lens as the main storage site
mc.answer: Promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production
mc.explanation: The liver supplies glucose to circulation.

writing.prompt: Compare the response after a meal with the response between meals. Include alpha/beta cells, insulin/glucagon, liver action and feedback.
writing.model: After a meal, higher glucose stimulates beta-cell insulin, supporting uptake and storage and reducing glucose output. Between meals, falling glucose supports alpha-cell glucagon, promoting liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production. Each response opposes the initiating change.

writing.prompt: Compare diabetes mellitus with diabetes insipidus using their hormone mechanism rather than their shared symptoms.
writing.model: Diabetes mellitus involves inadequate insulin production/action and elevated glucose; glucose in the urine can increase water loss. Diabetes insipidus involves impaired water conservation, often from ADH deficiency or resistance, producing excessive dilute urine without requiring high glucose.
criteria: Shared symptoms do not imply same cause

requiredChecks.title: Integrated chapter review and final check

options: TSH: thyroid / adrenal medulla
Insulin: liver / posterior pituitary
Cortisol: hypothalamus / pancreas
ADH: hypothalamus / posterior pituitary
mc.explanation: Production and release are separate parts of the ADH pathway.

mc.prompt: Which observation best fits primary thyroid underproduction with intact control?
options: Low T4 with elevated TSH
High T4 with low TSH proves pituitary failure
Only insulin changes
Low T4 always requires low TSH
mc.explanation: Low thyroid output reduces feedback inhibition of TSH secretion.
mc.cue: Use the stated location of failure.

mc.prompt: Which response directly follows sympathetic stimulation of the adrenal medulla?
options: Cortisol production in the cochlea
Insulin through ACTH
Aldosterone through TSH
Epinephrine and norepinephrine release
mc.explanation: The medulla links sympathetic neural signals with catecholamine hormone release.

mc.prompt: A normally responsive kidney receives more ADH. Which urine change is expected?
options: No possible change in water handling
Higher glucose production in the lens
Lower volume and higher concentration
Higher volume and lower concentration
mc.explanation: More water is reabsorbed from the tubule.

mc.prompt: Which explanation of low blood calcium is appropriate?
options: Insulin is always the main correction
Calcitonin is the only response that raises calcium
The pituitary must convert glucose into calcium
Increased PTH helps conserve and mobilize calcium
mc.answer: Increased PTH helps conserve and mobilize calcium
mc.explanation: PTH supports bone mobilization, kidney conservation and indirect intestinal absorption.

mc.prompt: Which statement about diabetes is most defensible?
options: Type 1 occurs only in children
Diabetes insipidus always requires high glucose
Type 2 means no insulin is ever present
Insulin deficiency and insulin resistance can both impair glucose regulation
mc.answer: Insulin deficiency and insulin resistance can both impair glucose regulation
mc.explanation: Mechanism is more informative than a rigid age or symptom rule.

writing.prompt: Compare three responses: water loss, a carbohydrate-containing meal and an immediate threat. For each, name a relevant trigger, hormone source, target, effect and control relationship.
writing.model: Water loss/concentration change can increase posterior-pituitary ADH, changing kidney water permeability and conserving water. A meal can increase pancreatic beta-cell insulin, supporting tissue uptake and liver storage to lower glucose. Immediate threat can activate sympathetic neurons and adrenal-medulla catecholamines, supporting rapid fuel and cardiovascular responses.

writing.prompt: Correct this explanation: “ACTH controls every adrenal hormone; all hormones act on every cell; and low thyroxine always means high TSH.” Include the conditions that make your corrections necessary.
writing.model: ACTH chiefly supports cortisol secretion; aldosterone is mainly controlled by angiotensin II and potassium, while the medulla receives sympathetic input. Targets require suitable receptors. Low thyroxine produces high TSH in primary thyroid failure only when the pituitary can respond; upstream failure can produce a different pattern.

worked.label: Worked example
worked.title: Compare after a meal with between meals
worked.scenario: Compare a rise in blood glucose after eating with a fall between meals.
steps: After a meal, beta cells release more insulin. Glucose uptake and storage help lower blood glucose.
Between meals, alpha cells release more glucagon. The liver releases glucose, helping raise blood glucose.
Both responses oppose their starting changes, so both use negative feedback.

guided.label: Practise with support
guided.title: Complete the two loops
guided.instruction: Choose the response that opposes the stated starting change.

items.prompt: Blood glucose rises → ____ → increased uptake and storage.
options: The posterior pituitary releases ADH
Beta cells release insulin
Alpha cells release glucagon
items.hint: High blood glucose is the trigger.
items.explanation: Insulin from beta cells promotes processes that lower the elevated blood glucose.

items.answer: Liver glycogen breakdown and glucose release
options: Glucose is removed from blood only to make more glycogen
All glucose is trapped inside beta cells
Liver glycogen breakdown and glucose release
items.hint: The response needs to raise blood glucose.
items.explanation: Glucagon promotes liver glucose release, opposing the original fall.

mc.prompt: A case states that the anterior pituitary cannot release enough TSH, while the thyroid could respond to stimulation. Which prediction follows?
mc.answer: Thyroxine can be low because the stimulating signal is insufficient
options: Thyroxine stays normal because reduced TRH directly stimulates the thyroid
Thyroxine rises because low TSH directly stimulates thyroid cells
Thyroxine rises because weak feedback guarantees increased TSH
Thyroxine can be low because the stimulating signal is insufficient
mc.explanation: Reduced TSH can limit thyroid output. The defect is in the stimulating signal, not necessarily the thyroid’s ability to respond.

mc.prompt: Which observation most directly distinguishes aldosterone action from ADH action?
mc.answer: Increased kidney sodium reabsorption rather than a direct increase in water permeability
options: Increased kidney sodium reabsorption rather than a direct increase in water permeability
Reduced collecting-duct water permeability despite unchanged sodium handling
Reduced kidney sodium reabsorption while potassium reabsorption increases
A direct increase in collecting-duct water permeability rather than sodium reabsorption
mc.explanation: The immediate kidney action differs: aldosterone affects sodium/potassium handling, while ADH directly affects water permeability.

mc.prompt: A case describes high blood glucose because target tissues respond poorly to insulin, even though insulin is still present. What is the key mechanism?
mc.answer: Reduced target response to the hormone
options: Excessive insulin-driven glucose uptake by target tissues
Insufficient insulin release from pancreatic beta cells
Reduced target response to the hormone
Increased target sensitivity to insulin
mc.explanation: The stated problem is insulin resistance. Hormone presence alone does not guarantee a normal target response.

writing.prompt: A case states that cortisol is low because the adrenal cortex cannot respond normally, while the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary are functioning. Predict ACTH and explain the feedback. Then explain why the rapid adrenal-medulla pathway is a different route.
writing.model: Low cortisol reduces feedback inhibition of the functioning hypothalamus and pituitary, so ACTH tends to rise. The cortex defect can still prevent adequate cortisol output. The rapid pathway uses sympathetic neurons to stimulate the adrenal medulla, which releases epinephrine and norepinephrine; it does not use ACTH as its main incoming signal.
criteria: ACTH tends to rise despite low cortical output
